records.our_prose: Honeydew is a heat-loving, long-season trailing melon (Cucumis melo, Inodorus Group) grown for its smooth-skinned, sweet, pale flesh, a warm-season cousin of cantaloupe, cucumber, and squash. Of the common melons it wants the most heat and the longest season, roughly 85 to 100 warm days, and it is more cold-sensitive than cantaloupe, so cool-summer northern and coastal areas are marginal to unsuitable. It is harvested once at full ripeness and does not sweeten further off the vine, so reading the plant is the whole game, and it is harder to read than cantaloupe. Unlike cantaloupe, honeydew does NOT slip from the vine, so ripeness is a learned judgment from several signs together: the smooth rind turns from green to a creamy white or yellow, its surface shifts from hard and slick to waxy and slightly tacky, the blossom end softens slightly and gives a faint sweet aroma, and the ground spot pales to cream. Because it will not detach on its own, cut the fruit from the vine. Plant only into warm soil above 70°F, give full sun and room to sprawl, and rely on bees for fruit set. The main pressures are cucumber beetles (which transmit bacterial wilt, to which melons are very susceptible), aphids, and spider mites, plus Fusarium wilt, powdery and downy mildew, and gummy stem blight.

records.our_prose: Honeydew is a moderate feeder that wants more phosphorus and potassium than nitrogen, since excess nitrogen drives leafy vine at the expense of fruit set and sugar. Work a lower-nitrogen complete fertilizer such as 5-10-10 into the bed before planting (Clemson suggests about 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet), then side-dress with a nitrogen source as the vines begin to run, and again lightly at flowering. Ease off nitrogen once fruit has set so the plant pours its energy into sizing and sweetening the melons rather than growing more vine. Because honeydew hangs on the vine longer than cantaloupe, pair feeding with steady, even moisture, since the nutrients only help a plant that is not also drought-stressed.
